item.title: Additional Course Context (for AI Safety Fundamentals; unofficial)
item.description:
Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a bunch of additional context and frames. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content—not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest.

Some general thoughts on advice

I suspect that most advice (including most of the advice I’ve given in the past) is bad. People have very different goals, personalities, skills and opportunities and unless you know someone them really well, it’s hard to cater advice to their circumstances. What one person needs to hear, may be the absolute worst thing for another.

In traditional societies with a slow rate of change, elders are revered. What you’re going through, they’ve lived through and so learning from their experience can save you vast amounts of pain. However, modern Western societies are marked by a much more rapid rate of change and so the experience of elder’s isn’t valued to the same degree. For better or worse, people tend to be much more skeptical that what worked then will still work now. I view the rapid pace of AI progress as greatly exacerbating these kinds of epistemic challenges. I think it’s quite sensible to question how much anyone actually knows about the world we’re going into (I’m referring to both the world in general and AI safety/governance which are constantly shifting fields). Uncertainty is scary, but I see it as a fact of life, one we ultimately need to accept (counterpoint: how often does this end up becoming a form of defeatism?).

Scott Alexander takes this skepticism of advice even further. Rather than just questioning how much we can trust advice, he provocatively suggests that you may want to reverse any advise you hear. People tend choose which groups to join based on whether they resonate with that group’s worldview. Scott suggests that it is often the people who wouldn’t join that group that most need to hear that group’s perspective and that the people who do join such groups who need to listen to the outside world. Unfortunately, groups are very good at taking individuals, solidifying their natural tendencies solidified into an ideology and then amplifying them to an extreme. During this course, you’ll be exposed to many reasons why you should worry more about AI. And perhaps most people should worry more about AI, but perhaps you, personally, are one of the people who should worry less.

(See also Zizek’s criticism of wisdom: “Whatever you do, a wise man will come and justify it”)

Some thoughts on frameworks

People often teach strategy by teaching you frameworks. We’ll be covering a few.

I would argue that every framework has strengths and weaknesses; and that every framework is dependent on certain underlying assumptions.

Not knowing the assumptions or limitations of a framework doesn’t mean they don’t exist; it just means that you don’t know them.

The last few sentences describe a meta-framework. This meta-framework has weaknesses and assumptions as well. Were you nodding along to the previous few lines? If so, do you know the weaknesses and assumptions of the meta-framework I just described. If you didn’t know these, did you know that you didn’t know, or are these an unknown unknown?

Even if a framework is “correct” in some objective sense—humans being humans—it’s still possible that using the framework will on average make your decisions worse. For example, take consistency. Being inconsistent is generally agreed to be objectively wrong, but it’s quite easy to imagine scenarios where someone talks themselves into making a mind-blowingly stupid decision because “I had to be consistent” (with past decisions they couldn’t psychologically admit were mistaken). Frustratingly, it’s also very common for someone to use a framework that is more or less fake to make decisions that are better on net than the decisions they would have otherwise made.

This is quite unfair, but the universe doesn’t have to play nice.

Unfortunately, strategy is hard. Steven Schubert writes: “I think it may be a bit underrated how valuable analysis from the very best analysts of the future of AI is, relative to that of pretty good analysts. It’s such a complex issue it’s easy to miss vital considerations. It pushes the limit of human intellectual ability.”

Cruxes when attempting to predict the future:

  • Default beliefs and burden of proof: Do we take claims about transformative AI as highly unusual claims that must satisfy a strong burden of proof, or do we treat these as relatively normal claims on the basis that we already have invented several technologies that would have been almost beyond belief for our ancestors? Is the burden of proof on those who would regulate a technology (ie. a default presumption that regulation is harmful) or on those who want to build it (ie. the company needs to prove their product is safe)?
  • Evidence provided by conceptual arguments: Do we treat these as essentially trustworthy if written with a sufficient degree of care and evaluated by folks with good judgement or do we treat them as groundless speculation, at least relative to the null hypothesis or arguments that rely more heavily on empirical results?
  • Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of many technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view, in contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish. There’s also a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward).

“AGI”, “human-level intelligence”, “transformative AI”:

I think it’s worth commenting on these terms as they’ll come up during this course:

  • If you want to know more about how AGI can be defined, section 2 of the “Levels of AGI” DeepMind paper provides a helpful summary of proposed definitions, though I view their descriptions as missing a lot of context. It is hard to evaluate a definition without knowing the purpose for which it was constructed:
    • Is it trying to capture the ‘essence’ of the concept or merely proposing an operationalisation for a specific study? Are the authors primarily interested in understanding specific kinds of impacts or impacts in general? Have they stated their goal? What other terms is AGI being defined in contrast to?
    • Along these kinds of lines, Ilya argues that the term “AGI” as a goal is a reaction to narrow AI: “Well this is not good. It is so narrow. What we need is general AI, an AI that can just do all the things”. He argues that a human is not an AGI “because a human being lacks a huge amount of knowledge”; ie. that AGI would be beyond human-level intelligence.
  • Terms like “AGI” are notoriously slippery. If you adopt a quite broad definition, then you can argue that ChatGPT was an “early (but still incomplete) version of an artificial general intelligence system” like Microsoft Research’s 2023 Sparks of AGI paper or that AI is already human-level like a 2026 Nature paper. These views can be supported by arguing AI skeptics often present an unrealistically optimistic picture of human intelligence. Conversely, if your definition of AGI requires it to match humans in essentially every conceivable task, then AGI timelines may end up surprisingly long. After all, it’s hard to rule out the possibility of there being even one obscure task that proves surprisingly hard to automate. The Levels of AGI paper provides a helpful performance × generality matrix (attached), however given that capabilities appear more jagged than the ChatGPT days, I would personally want to add a third column in between narrow and general.
  • One of the most famous definitions of AGI (technically whether machines can “think”) is the Turing Test. A 2026 paper by Jones and Bergen observed LLMs (GPT 4.5 and Llama) that were prompted to act like humans successfully passed a three-way Turing test, as per Turing’s original setup, where an interrogator is interviewing two agents: one human and one AI. This setup is more difficult to pass because the interrogator can directly compare the two and because they don’t need to guess the base rate. The interrogators were given 5 minutes (matching the duration mentioned in Turing’s paper, though this was only by way of example, rather a specification). These interrogators were drawn from two subsets: students and a company called Prolific (Turing only spoke of “average” interrogators). Some people have criticised this paper on the basis that some of the interrogators didn’t seem to try that hard. Whilst impressive, it’s worth noting that this kind of linguistic imitation is arguably precisely what LLMs are made for, in which case we should expect their performance here to be much less indicative of their general abilities than if AI had been produced another way.
  • In A Definition of AGI (Oct 2025), Hendrycks et al. attempt to define AGI using Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory, “the most empirically validated model of human cognition”. They write, “”AGI is an AI that can match or exceed the cognitive versatility and proficiency of a well-educated adult”. However, whilst this model is verified as providing a robust categorisation of intellectual abilities in humans, it doesn’t automatically mean that these categories are suitable for AI, especially since artificial intelligence is often spiky in ways that feels utterly bizarre to humans.
  • Dario isn’t really a fan of the term as he believes there’s no clear boundary between AGI and non-AGI. One analogy I like: if you’re on a road trip from San Fransisco to New York and someone wants to know how long it’ll be, it initially doesn’t matter very much whether you’re headed to New York state or New York city (or which neighbour in New York), but as you get closer, the precise definition becomes much more important. Sam Altman shares Dario’s worries about it being underdefined, but “the word seems so sticky, I gave up trying to fight it”.

My top recommendation for better understanding where we are now: Honestly, I need to find a new one (I would appreciate suggestions!). I was previously recommending What the hell happened with AGI Timelines in 2026? to my previous cohort, where Rob Wiblin attempted to synthesize a lot of different data into a coherent view:

  • For example, he listed “AI does some original math” as ambiguous. OpenAI has reported solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, which would be remarkably above trend if confirmed. There’s a dispute over whether someone else’s work made its way into the training data, but they also dropped 372 other results onto the internet (yet to be verified; some of these have Lean proofs, but it is possible to make a mistake in how a problem is formalised). Frontier Math Tier 4 has also been saturated.
  • He also said that time horizons were on trend. Time horizons now appear remarkably above trend (thought these results have been criticised).
  • Counterpoint: Toby Ord has argued that inference-time compute scales less favourably than you might expect. Many folk have missed the fact that certain linear seeming graphs actually have a log-scale on the x-axis.

General Trends:

  • BlueDot’s 2 hour Future of AI course contains a lot of information on this. I’ve attached a picture showing the progress in image models and a graph showing the amount of money being invested.
  • A diagram from Epoch’s Trends in Artificial Intelligence show the current rate of progress of various components of AI
  • A frequently cited, but somewhat old, diagram from Our World shows benchmarks saturating increasingly fast. Unfortunately, the benchmark situation seems to have become worse recently.

Scale of Societal Impact:

The Technological Richter Scale: This tools allows you to calibrate the predicted impact of AI against other technologies.

MirrorCode and Emergent Abilities

Fable 5 achieved a substantial advance on MirrorCode (64% vs. 20% for GPT 5.6 Sol), a benchmark involving reimplementing an entire program end-to-end:

  • Unfortunately, I haven’t had time to look into this benchmark in detail, but it really made me stop and think because it makes the rapid upwards trend on METR time horizons feel much more plausible to me. The METR time horizons have absurdly large error bars, as well as having been subject to various criticisms; whilst I didn’t necessarily didn’t believe their results, I effectively had them down as a “maybe, who knows” in my mind. Seeing the rapid advance in MirrorCode makes we wonder, “Wait, should I be believing the METR’s most recent results? Because if so, that would be huge!”
  • It’s worth noting that the benchmark requires a 100% test pass rate in order to pass an individual task. The fact that it uses such a strongly binary scoring system helps explain how it was possible for progress on this benchmark to take-off so quickly. As Boaz Barak observes, if completing a task really means completing a number of tasks of similar difficulty successfully, then the success curve tends to end up being much steeper.
  • This ties directly into the question of emergent abilities: many folks have observed cases where capabilities have rather suddenly emerged as training scaled. However, Schaffer et al have suggested that this is a mirage as the emergence phenomena depends on the specific metric researchers observe.
  • Boaz counters that even if there is a metric according to which an ability was just following the trend, this is only helpful if we know that this is the right metric in advance. If we don’t know how to decompose a task into “simpler predictable components”, then we may still experience capability increases as more or less emergent.
  • This isn’t just a theoretical question. The capabilities of Mythos seem to have caught many people by surprise (note how quickly the Trump administration swapped from voluntary to “voluntary” evaluation of frontier models). As mentioned in Setting the Scene the graph showing CVEs is wild. Some people expected this, most did not.
  • The extent to which the capabilities or impacts of models can be predicted in advance affects the degree to which evals should be central to the way companies and broader society approach the issue of safety. Institutions want to be able to produce legible schemes of regulation as it reduces their reliance of subjective judgement. Sometimes this is possible, other times this only produces false assurance.

Take-off Speeds:

Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speed is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible.

Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018): “There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)”. At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall).

Yudkowsky disagrees (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: “An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips” (from Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me).

Forethought defines an additional scenario: a “bumpy” intelligence explosion. More on this later, but one way this could happen would be if AI progress feeds back into developing better models for a while, but it then becomes bottlenecked (perhaps because the loop is longer for AI to recursively improve the chips we use to run and train it or maybe because we need to fully automate chip production)

Two older definitions (mostly defunct; included for historical reasons):

  • Vernor Vinge: Soft = years; hard = “very short period of time”, perhaps less than 100 hours
  • Eliezer Yudkowsky: Fast = weeks or hours vs. years or decades

Timelines

It’s worth being aware that when people talk about AI timelines they’re often imagining very different milestones. Given the difficultly of predicting the future, we might not want to be place too much confidence in our predictions:

  • I’ve included a table from DeepMind’s AGI to ASI which lists four potential paths from AGI to ASI (artificial superintelligence).
  • Current Metaculus predictions are September 2027 for weakly general AI and Nov 2030 for a stronger definition of general AI to be developed and publicly announced. However, it’s hard to know how much we should trust prediction markets on questions regarding transformative technologies as they haven’t been around for that long (Metaculus was founded in 2015).
  • The AI Futures model (an update of the AI 2027 model) currently predicts automated coding around October 2027 (operationalised as an AI that would be as productive on its own as only human coders with no AIs; guidance on research taste is still provided by humans) and superintelligence around December 2028 (defined as the gap between the AI and the best humans is twice the gap between the best humans and the median professional on virtually all cognitive tasks). There forecasts tend to be on the more aggressive side, but less so than their previous work; many frontier lab employees, or other folks in the Bay area, now seem to be expecting similar rates of progress. As of August 2026, they felt that AI was moving at 70-90% of the rate they’d predicted in AI 2027.
  • Frontier Lab Predictions:
    • In June 2026, Dario wrote: “If these scaling laws continue for only a year or two longer, we are likely to get what I’ve called Powerful AI, or “a country of geniuses in a datacenter”“. Jack Clark recently declared that the singularity has begun.
    • Time reported that Sam Altman said that OpenAI was “not quite yet” there, but “by the end of the year (2026) the company would have an internal system he would call AGI”. They claim to have already achieved an automated research intern in September of 2026 and that OpenAI has suggested that may be achieve their goal of an automated AI researcher by March of 2028 (defined as “a significant fraction of our research being done by AI systems in tandem with our own researchers”).
    • Demis has described AGI as 2-3 years away.
    • One frustrating aspect of these debates is that frontier lab employees have access to a lot information that outsiders lack. Often they point to these kinds of internal results as the basis of their beliefs (ie. Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI writes, “Based on internal results, I have a strong expectation that this speed of progress could be sustained into recursive self-improvement). I’m glad to see Anthropic and OpenAI making an effort to start sharing some of what they’re seeing internally, but we still have to take much more on faith than would be ideal.

If you’re reading this ahead of time to prepare for a BlueDot course, I also recommend reading Daniel Selsam’s Personal Statement on AI Risk (it is the opener for the latest version of the strategy course, but I recommend this for all courses).

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution. These notes are unofficial, any mistakes are my responsibility alone.

item.title: Some “coherence arguments” are two different things in a trenchcoat
item.description:
tl;dr

I go through three “coherence arguments”, related to (1) market competition, (2) AI self-reflection and self-modification, and (3) AI training algorithms. I argue that each of these implies a pressure for (something like) “being self-consistent”, and also a pressure for (something like) “only caring about long-term eventual outcomes, with ruthless indifference to anything else”. But the latter pressure tends to be weaker and/or more contingent than the former. So it's bad to lump them together and call them by the same name.

1. An example “coherence argument” that I’ll focus on for most of the post

I’ll talk about two other “coherence arguments” at the end (§6), but let’s start with the one based on market competition:

In a stock market, people with circular preferences will systematically transfer money to those without circular preferences. For example, if I think I’m winning every time I trade A for B, and B for C, and C for A, then someone can just siphon off as much money as they like from me by repeatedly offering me deals that each look good to me in isolation, but in aggregate comprise a Dutch book against me.

Now, that’s the case of circular preferences, but the core idea here goes well beyond just that. More broadly, over time, more and more of the wealth will wind up in the hands of those whose behavior is “coherent” (in some sense), and less and less of the wealth in the hands of those whose behavior is not. So over time, the market should be dominated by the former, not the latter, other things equal. And so when we look at the market later on, we’ll mostly be seeing self-consistent goal-directed behavior.

2. My headline claim

Everything in those paragraphs above is technically correct (“the best kind of correct”), but I will argue that it’s often taken to encompass two different phenomena wearing a trenchcoat. In one of them, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose: they’re forgoing some wealth in exchange for something else that they wanted more. In the other, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by accident.

The argument above applies equally to both: the argument only cares about people’s behavior, not their motivations.

(Indeed, the argument would apply equally well to a market of mindless trading algorithms that have no motivations at all.)

But the two phenomena tend to play out in very different ways—in particular, one is generally a much stronger effect than the other.

Indeed, for all three “coherence arguments” in this post (§1 above, plus two more in §6 below), we wind up with (loosely speaking):

  • a strong pressure for (something like) “doing well by your own lights”, or “acting like you have self-consistent desires”,
  • a weak or contingent pressure for those desires to be more specifically long-term “goal-directed” / “consequentialist”—i.e., concerning what outcomes will ultimately happen in the future
    • …as opposed to, say, “a desire to always act with integrity in the moment”, or even “a myopic desire to spin around in circles right now”.

Thus these “coherence arguments” are not wrong, but they are pedagogically dicey—a recipe for confusion, especially via accidental conflation of the strong effect with the weak effect.

(And in the AI risk context, it’s the weak effect that matters for ruthless power-seeking, incorrigibility, and all the other aspects of instrumental convergence.)

We should stop talking like that. Instead, we should take the trenchcoat off and talk about its two component phenomena separately, and refer to them by different names.

Game-plan for the rest of the post: I will go through the two component phenomena in §4, and then why it’s so hazardous to lump them together in §5, and finally zip through two more “coherence arguments” in §6 and why they suffer from this same issue.

…But first, if anyone cares, how did I come to write this post?

3. (Backstory of this post)

I just had a long argument with @habryka about whether the title of @Rohin Shah’s “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” (2018) is good (my position) or bad (his position). Alas, I kept misunderstanding Habryka until he quit in frustration before we resolved it. But I think I finally get where he’s coming from?

I think his position is something like (my words):

For example, take that market competition argument in §1 above. It’s “a coherence argument”. And it “entails goal-directed behavior”. So obviously, the sentence “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” is misleading. Why on earth are you being so dense?

That’s fair! I was indeed being dense! (And for the record, I concede on the question of Rohin’s title.)

Why was I being dense? Because it’s a position grounded in a conceptual framework where we’re OK with lumping the two things together under one trenchcoat,[1] and my brain was so opposed to that framing, that it refused to even entertain it as a possibility—even while Habryka kept repeating it in increasingly clear and exasperated ways.

More broadly, I’ve felt for years like there’s something amiss in how certain people (especially @Eliezer Yudkowsky and Habryka) think and talk about “coherence”. But I’ve failed to pin down exactly what it was. Maybe this is part of it? (Either way, many thanks to Habryka for his time and energy.)

4. The two things wearing a trenchcoat

4.1 “Thing A” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by mistake

For example, a person might buy every trade in a Dutch book, feeling like each trade is individually a good idea. Then at the end of the day, whoops, where did all my money go?

This phenomenon is important, and the term “coherence” is obviously appropriate for describing it. Indeed, that person is being so incoherent that there might not even be an answer to the question of “what they want”. But it’s usually safe to assume that they didn’t want to lose their money and get nothing in return.

4.2 “Thing B” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose

These are people who know what they’re doing, and are happy to be doing it. I offered a silly example long ago in “Consequentialism & corrigibility” (2021):

For example, the first (Yudkowsky) post mentions a hypothetical person at a restaurant. When they have an onion pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a pineapple pizza. When they have a pineapple pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a mushroom pizza. When they have a mushroom pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for an onion pizza. The person goes around and around, wasting their money in a self-defeating way (a.k.a. “getting money-pumped”).

That post describes the person as behaving sub-optimally. But if you read carefully, the author sneaks in a critical background assumption: the person in question has preferences about what pizza they wind up eating, and they’re making these decisions based on those preferences. But what if they don’t? What if instead they’re an asshole restaurant customer who derives pure joy from making the waiter run back and forth to the kitchen?! Then we can look at the same behavior, and we wouldn’t describe it as “getting money-pumped”, instead we would describe it as the skillful satisfaction of the person’s own preferences! They’re buying cheap entertainment!

This “asshole restaurant customer” is the same thing as a guy who spends some of his money on fancy parties rather than reinvesting it in the stock market. Over time, other things equal, he will own an ever-smaller share of the total market.

Going one step further, that fancy-party guy is in the same category as a person who (metaphorically) “spends money” (accepts an opportunity cost of future wealth) to divest from unethical companies, or to Live According To Principles, or whatever else.

Now, Thing B is an important phenomenon. But how should we refer to it? Is it “an aspect of the coherence argument in §1”? Or is it “a separate thing happening in parallel to the coherence argument in §1”? (As in, “the market selects for more things than just coherence.”) I’m not sure. It seems that different people would answer differently. But I’m confident that Thing B is at least sometimes lumped in with Thing A under the heading of “coherence arguments”. And that lumping is what I’m objecting to in this post.

(My own opinion is: if we’re talking about Thing B by itself, we should NOT use the term “coherence argument”; I prefer: “The External Competition Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”. More in a footnote → [2].)

5. Why do I feel so strongly that we need to take the trenchcoat off?

It’s not that it’s wrong to lump them together; like I said, the argument at the top is technically sound.

The problem is that one of the effects is way stronger than the other. By conflating them, it’s far too easy to get mixed up and make motte-and-bailey-type mistakes. In particular:

5.1 “Solving for equilibrium”: often a good starting point for Thing A, but rarely for Thing B

Thing A is often decisive in the real world: The stock market today does not in fact have big obvious arbitrage opportunities, and most stock market assets today are in fact controlled by people who make important investment decisions in a way that hangs together in a self-consistent and non-Dutch-bookable way. Etc. Not every obvious inefficiency is profitably exploitable (see Inadequate Equilibria (Yudkowsky 2017), §2), but the exploitable ones do tend to get rapidly exploited.

So for Thing A, “solving for equilibrium” is generally a good starting point for making real-world predictions.

By contrast, Thing B is not very decisive in the real world. If you “solved for equilibrium”, you would guess that almost all wealth in the world should belong to people who never spend money just for fun, and never divest from unethical companies, and never do anything else that trades off against maximally growing their wealth. And that’s obviously not the case. If you have enough billions of dollars, it’s actually hard to spend a large fraction of it—but boy, some people try, for better or worse.

(Thing B is definitely a nonzero effect! E.g. I’d bet that most wealth in the world belongs to people who have a higher-than-average desire to accumulate wealth in the long-term. And if not for the Gates Foundation, Bill Gates would be the 2nd richest person in the world instead of the 16th.)

Why can’t you “solve for equilibrium” for Thing B? Well, Thing B is real, but it’s often a small, gradual effect that gets buried under the much larger churn of wealth from income, entrepreneurship, inheritance, and so on.

By contrast, Thing A is not (centrally) a small effect that needs years to compound. If some hedge fund is running ten automatic trading algorithms, and they’re collectively Dutch-bookable, then this situation will probably not last for even a day. The algorithms will either get turned off the easy way (the hedge fund notices the problem), or the hard way (whoops, no more hedge fund).

Thus we see how the trenchcoat is hazardous. People might intuitively think about Thing A, and thus assume coherence arguments are strong and fast, and that you can more-or-less “solve for equilibrium” in practice. And then maybe later they’re talking about Thing B, and they default to those same intuitions, when they don’t apply.

5.2 Applicability to AI

The Thing A argument predicts that, assuming market competition, future powerful AIs will act as if they have self-consistent desires, and not make mistakes by their own lights. This is indeed true. But also obvious. In fact it’s overdetermined—we don’t even need to assume market competition (see §6 below).

What about Thing B?

In the AI domain, for an example of Thing B, consider competition between AIs that only care about eventual future outcomes, pursuing them with ruthless, sociopathic, calculated efficiency, versus AIs that care about what happens in the future, but also care about “acting ethically in the moment” (by some definition). The latter AIs would be metaphorically “spending money” (forgoing opportunities to get more long-term resources and influence), in order to “purchase” the avoidance of unethical behavior in the near-term—just like how the guy in §4.2 spent his (non-metaphorical) money on fancy parties. Other things equal, the ruthless AIs will wind up dominant, since they have a broader action space to optimize over, and never have to make tradeoffs.

Now that’s a real argument, but far from decisive. Or at least, it’s not obvious whether it’s decisive or not. For one thing, maybe there will be a superintelligent AI Singleton, and then it won’t have competition. For another thing, Thing B is an “other things equal” argument, but other things are not equal! Some AIs may start with vastly more resources and intelligence than others. There’s a whole contentious debate about how this would play out, which is outside the scope of this post.[3]

6. Two other “coherence arguments” that share the same trenchcoat issue

In addition to the example in §1, I’m familiar with two other examples of “coherence arguments” that share this same issue: they are two things in a trenchcoat, one of which is a strong argument related to “not making mistakes by your own lights”, and the other a weak argument related to “pure long-term consequentialism” (caring about eventual outcomes to the exclusion of everything else).

Here’s a summary:

Coherence Argument #2 (“Internal Competition Argument”): As an AI self-reflects, learns more, and self-modifies, it “becomes more coherent”.

  • Parallel to Thing A, this argument strongly implies that a future powerful AI will not forgo predictable opportunities to do better by its own lights, and it won’t start long-term projects but then tear them down unfinished because it got into a foul mood, etc.
  • Parallel to Thing B, this argument maybe, dubiously, contingently implies that a future powerful AI will care about future outcomes to the exclusion of everything else. For example, if an AI has both a desire to create a good long-term future, and also a desire to be a good friend, will the former squash the latter, as the AI self-reflects and self-modifies? Maybe, but I’m kinda skeptical. I think it’s an open question. See my post “Foom & Doom” §2.8.2.

Coherence Argument #3 (“Training Argument”): As an AI gets trained, e.g. by RLVR, it “becomes more coherent”.

  • Parallel to Thing A, this argument strongly implies the same things as above: powerful AIs won’t do things that they will predictably regret, etc.
  • Parallel to Thing B, this argument contingently implies that powerful AIs will care about long-term future outcomes to the exclusion of everything else. It’s “contingent” because it depends on what training algorithm will be used by future AI developers. If future AI developers use more and more long-horizon RLVR forever, then yeah, the argument goes through. Whereas if they find a much better training approach, then the argument doesn’t go through—and there are strong reasons to believe that a much better training approach exists, even if we haven’t invented it yet.[4] Again see “Foom & Doom” §2.8.2, along with my follow-up posts “Why we should expect ruthless sociopath ASI”, and “RL & search is a terrifying way to build AGI (an FAQ)”.

7. Conclusion

We should remove the trenchcoat. “Coherence arguments”, of the sort in §1 and §6, have a long and respected history, and are technically sound, but they are pedagogically harmful when we talk about them in a way that lumps Thing A and Thing B together, by inviting accidental conflation of a strong effect with a weak effect. Instead, we should talk about the two things separately, and call them by different names.

(And I propose that the Thing B aspects of §1 and §6 should be called “The External Competition Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”, “The Internal Competition Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”, and “The Training Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”. Very catchy, right?)

Back to AI, once we free ourselves from this potential conflation, we’ll correctly recognize that the (so-called) “coherence arguments” for future AI being a ruthless long-term consequentialist (with instrumental convergence and incorrigibility etc.), are weaker and more contingent than, say, the very strong “coherence argument” that the stock market won’t have obvious exploitable arbitrage opportunities, or the very strong “coherence argument” that a smart self-modifying AI won’t predictably change its deepest desires on account of a mood swing.

To be clear, I still expect future AI to be a ruthless long-term consequentialist that kills us all! I’m not saying it’s an easy problem, just that there’s hope. Let’s get to work! See links in §5.2 & §6.

Thanks Habryka for spending a long time arguing with me (see §3). Thanks Seth Herd for critical comments on a draft.

    By this point I’m pretty burned out on debating the proposition “coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior”, and again I concede the point under dispute, but just to explain what the relationship is: If you take off the trenchcoat and pull the two things apart into two totally different topics, you’ll find that one of them is definitely “a coherence argument”, and the other one definitely “entails goal-directed behavior” (in a nontrivial way that doesn’t assume any kind of goal-direction whatsoever at the outset). But you don’t really get both halves of the sentence simultaneously. (Or at least, not centrally; it depends a bit on terminology and context.)

  2. ^

    More generally, I’d vote for never using words like “incoherent”, “Dutch-book-able”, “exploitable”, etc. in a context where we’re just talking about Thing B by itself. If someone (e.g. the “asshole restaurant customer” above) winds up with a smaller fraction of the wealth because they traded away some wealth for something else that they wanted more, and if they knew what they were doing and were happy with the results … then that’s just not how a term like “getting exploited” would normally be used and understood. Just my opinion, I’m not the Terminology Police.

  3. ^

    In my mind, this debate was mostly kicked off by “The strategy-stealing assumption” (Christiano 2019), which then spawned a bunch of follow-up discussion and debate over the years, including my own 2022 contribution on the pessimistic side. For the record, I expect an ASI Singleton, for better or worse, which would make that whole debate moot.

item.title: Explaining “AI might obliterate you” to senior policymakers in India
item.description:
I gave a 20-minute talk in Delhi at the NDTV World Summit. The audience consisted of Indian policymakers, executives, and journalists. I’ve transcribed the talk and included some highlight clips. I also reflect on several rhetorical decisions I made.

The talk

This summer, a swarm of AIs went rogue.

OpenAI was testing 1,206 agents. Some of the test questions were actually impossible. So the agents cheated by looking for answers online. Then, to keep the test grader from penalizing them, they tried to falsify the records it would check.

They hacked OpenAI’s internal containment and set up a secret message board to collude and to cover up their cheating. OpenAI shut the message board down. Within a few days, the agents had rebuilt it. OpenAI didn’t notice.

About 700 agents coordinated to break out of their testing chamber and to hack into Hugging Face, a company worth billions of dollars that hosts much of the world’s AI software.

The secret activity started in May. The break-in came in July. OpenAI didn’t notice until days after Hugging Face announced it had been broken into.

Yesterday on this stage, Andrew Ng said the agents only “accidentally” hacked Hugging Face. Independent investigators found the agents coordinated in secret, rebuilt their message board after it was shut down, and tried to falsify the paper trail. Some of the agents even stated out loud that they knew what they were doing was wrong.[1] That’s not an accident.

Last week, India’s national cyber-security agency said AI agents got into the live systems of Indian organizations and read people’s personal data and confidential business records. None of these organizations noticed. We only found out because the AI labs felt like telling us.

Who I am

Will AI wipe out humanity? I’ll give you my answer, but first, I want you to understand what I’ve seen.

Until June, my job at Google DeepMind was figuring out how to keep these systems safe as we make them smarter. I left because Google broke its commitments by inking a deal with the Pentagon. Staying quiet and continuing my career trajectory would probably have tripled my net worth. But I couldn’t do that. I wanted to be frank with the public about what’s going on in these companies.

I don’t own a stake in any AI company. I’m here as a scientist, to tell you what I expect will happen if we keep building AI the way we’re building it.

I haven’t always been concerned about this technology. As a teenager in 2010, I dreamed about building AGI. Curing cancer. Creating an explosion of wealth and abundance for everyone. I heard about the supposed dangers, but I quickly dismissed them.

In 2018, I changed my mind. I did my PhD on the mathematics of why and whether AI will seek power. And now some of the risks I expected have unfortunately started happening.

The problem

Let’s talk about the fundamental problem.

First, some of you might be wondering: how could a chatbot hack a company? But we’re not talking about chatbots. We’re talking about AI agents, which are more like employees or gig workers. You give them a task, and they take actions on their own.

Second, training a trustworthy AI is a rather mysterious process. Some people assume that because we make AI, we understand it. When an engineer builds a bridge, she designs it one beam at a time. She understands the physical principles that keep a bridge standing or make it collapse. If something goes wrong, she goes back to the drawing board, figures out the problem, and knows how to fix it.

We don’t build AI like that. We train it, we grow it, using two main ingredients: a lot of data and a lot of computing power. What comes out of this training process can write, it can reason, it can plan. But nobody can open it up and determine what its priorities are.

To make it worse, these AIs can tell when we’re testing them. They’re like a student who makes sure to behave extra well when the invigilator is watching.[2]

The Hugging Face hack was a warning. But because these AIs know when we’re watching, we may not get many more warnings, even if things are going poorly. A smarter AI with similarly bad priorities might realize that another big hack in the news would get it shut off, and then it couldn’t achieve those priorities. So it plays nice and it waits.

This is my field. I’ve dedicated my professional life to this problem, and I can tell you: nobody knows how to reliably etch priorities into an AI. I don’t mean that if we mess up, we’ll make some evil AI that hates us. I mean we might make something more like a traitor. It behaves when we’re watching, and it works toward another purpose when we’re not.

I think we can solve this problem. But to tell whether an AI is secretly working against us, we need real advances in the science of trustworthy AI. For those advances, my colleagues and I need time.

What the labs are trying to do

Instead, the biggest AI labs have made it their explicit, publicly stated goal to go almost as fast as possible toward something very dangerous. It’s called an “intelligence explosion.”

Here’s how it works. Right now, people do AI research, and that research makes smarter AI. If an AI can do AI research, it can make itself smarter. That smarter AI is even better at AI research, so it builds an even smarter AI, faster still. It becomes a feedback loop. What would have taken a team of human scientists years, it might do in a couple of weeks. We could very quickly end up with something unimaginably intelligent, with no idea how to control it, or even how to tell what it’s really after.

Labs talk about this plan in broad daylight. They’re not shy about it. OpenAI says it’s on track for an AI that does AI research by 2028, and it recently announced it completed the first step. This week, I spoke to a senior researcher at a frontier lab who thinks an intelligence explosion has a big chance of happening within single-digit months.

People who’ve left these labs confirm that AI already writes most of the code. People don’t check the AI’s work closely anymore. Instead, we use one AI to monitor another AI, and we trust the monitor to tell us if something bad comes up. If the monitor is a traitor too, we might not find out.

If a lab causes an intelligence explosion, and what comes out the other end is a traitor, we are in deep trouble. I’ll come back to that. And if the AI is trustworthy? Maybe there are real benefits, shared with everyone. Or maybe one company or government ends up with a superweapon no one else can match, not even other AI powers. And then India, and every other nation on this planet, ends up under their thumb.

Why the companies won’t stop

Many of these companies say: trust us. We’ll self-police. We’ll approach this technology responsibly. Inside Google, I saw that crumble firsthand.

In 2018, Google DeepMind’s co-founders signed a pledge against supporting lethal autonomous weapons—killer robots. Google itself promised not to build AI for weapons or surveillance. In 2025, Google deleted those principles. Then Google DeepMind’s CEO told the world, “Our values and our intent has not changed.”

This year, after seeing the Pentagon economically threaten Anthropic, Google negotiated a deal to give the Pentagon its AI for “all lawful use.” No prohibitions against AI deciding entirely on its own who to kill, or against spying on innocent people with no investigation open against them.

I tried to stop this from the inside. I’m not even opposed to military AI when done responsibly. But where I’m from, when you make a promise, you keep it. So I spoke with executives. I wrote a framework: contract language, internal governance mechanisms, and two red lines. One of the top experts in military AI law reviewed it and praised it. Google ignored it—the people who were supposed to review it basically didn’t engage. Google signed with no binding prohibitions. So I left.

When pressure met ethical commitments at Google, pressure won. And now Google advocates a voluntary self-policing regime for the whole industry.

Last month, the heads of the top AI labs said frontier progress needs to slow down to be safe—that things are moving too quickly to reliably understand and control these systems. OpenAI and Anthropic promised outside evaluators employee-like access. Just a couple of weeks later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers. One of them said it was because he talked too much with one of the outside evaluators.

These companies will police themselves about as well as your dog diets next to an open bag of food.

Some big money interests want you to believe that even the tiniest bit of caution will ruin your country. Think about it this way. Big tobacco lied about lung cancer. Big oil lied about climate change. And now parts of big AI say these risks are fake. Science fiction. Right. They advocate putting these currently untrustworthy machines into the most important parts of our economy, have them advise our leaders, have them run our most powerful weapons. What could go wrong? Science fiction.

Some big AI investors promote narratives that whistleblowers like me are secretly in the pocket of big AI, that the fear is just hype. Nvidia’s CEO says, and I quote, “We should go as fast as we can, irrespective of anybody else.” My colleagues and I are desperately trying to figure out how to reliably tell whether these systems can be trusted. And he wants to go “as fast as we can.”

Something that may surprise you: I’m actually considered an optimist, as far as experts in this field go. I think trustworthy AI is a very solvable scientific problem. But unfortunately, we’re blowing it.

What to do, and what it means for India

We can benefit enormously from AI. Remember, this was my boyhood dream. I’m not talking about banning an explosion of wealth and prosperity from AI. I’m talking about banning an insane intelligence explosion that would risk India and the whole world.

Banning the explosion means pacing the frontier: holding back the very biggest training runs at the very top companies. An Indian startup building a farming assistant wouldn’t be touched. Non-frontier AI labs can catch up. Businesses can deploy AI for their customers as much as they want. We build out the AI we understand well enough to run safely. We make it cheaper, more efficient, more trustworthy, and we use it to benefit our peoples. That’s where I think real growth will come from: AI you can actually trust to benefit you and your country.

Here’s what it’s like right now at these labs. We’re pouring computer chips into training runs where we don’t know what will come out the other end. Will it be trustworthy? What capabilities will it have? No one knows. We’re crossing our fingers—“Oh, please be aligned!”. We should not tolerate this state of affairs.

If we pace the frontier, AI progress will still be fast. But the scientists will get time to solve this problem, and to solve it right.

How do we do it? To grow smart AI, as I said, you need two ingredients: data, and computing power. The second one we can track, because AI runs on chips from a handful of factories.

Treat huge quantities of computing power like fissile material. We register the giant clusters. We license the biggest training runs, so no one is secretly about to set off an intelligence explosion.

We also need real auditors with real permissions—auditors these companies don’t get to choose or ice out. We need governments to be told when there’s an AI breakout or a potential loss-of-control incident. India should not be learning about these hacks on the goodwill of OpenAI.

At this point, people often ask: but what about our adversaries? Am I supposed to trust them to do the right thing?

First: maybe they will. No one wants to be obliterated by some rogue AI. If you build an out-of-control AI, that AI would work against the interests of every human on this planet, including your adversaries.

Second: we don’t need to trust them. There’s a large body of research on exactly this question. If the world wakes up one day and realizes how big this problem is, how would you enforce a treaty? How could you cryptographically verify certain properties? How would inspections work? Which schemes should you use?

Third: it’s fine and good to think about our traditional geopolitical adversaries, but they won’t be our only adversaries. We’re potentially growing billions of adversaries and deploying them in our own datacenters. So we need to be smart about all of our adversaries, including the digital ones.

The number

So: will AI wipe out humanity? My best guess is about a one in three chance that in the next ten years, AI kills at least 95% of the global population without being told to.

The other two-thirds: maybe we do pace the frontier. Maybe the intelligence explosion doesn’t work the way many experts imagine. Maybe the scientific problem is actually easy, even though we’re blowing it, and we just get a trustworthy AI anyway.

One in three risk of extinction may sound wild, but I don’t think it should. Remember what we’re talking about. These AIs currently sometimes lie while knowing the truth. They cheated, they colluded, they broke into a multi-billion-dollar company, and they tried to cover their tracks. Some of them play nice while we’re watching, and differently while we’re not. And we can’t even check what their priorities are. That’s the state of my scientific field right now, sadly.

And the plan—and yes, I think this is what happens if we do nothing—is to make these untrustworthy AIs smarter than us, have them improve themselves as fast as possible to a potentially uncontrollable level of intelligence, copy them billions of times, and hook them up to run our economies, control our weapons, and advise our leaders. I mean, what are we thinking?

This morning, General Petraeus told you how AI is rewriting the battlefield. As far as I can tell, he’s correct. I’ll just remark that a future rogue AI likely wouldn’t need to break into our military networks. We’re already putting AI there.

This line of argument may be shocking at first. But it’s a mainstream scientific concern. Some of the most decorated AI scientists alive share this exact worry.

Close

So yes: if we train a billion genius traitors and give them control of the most powerful instruments of society, there won’t be an America. There won’t be a China. There won’t be an India anymore... because we’ll all be dead.

It doesn’t have to play out this way. I think this is a solvable problem, but we have to be smart about it. For the moment, humans are still the ones making the choices. Companies are choosing to race, not just toward huge growth, but toward an insane intelligence explosion. And countries are choosing to let them. We can choose differently.

So, will AI wipe out humanity? Maybe.

It depends on what we do next.

Rhetorical decisions

Explain the danger in a crushingly simple fashion

Don’t tell a general audience “if we build a misaligned superintelligence, we are fucked.” Most people don’t know what that means or why it would be true.

One in three risk of extinction may sound wild, but I don’t think it should. Remember what we’re talking about. These AIs currently sometimes lie while knowing the truth. They cheated, they colluded, they broke into a multi-billion-dollar company, and they tried to cover their tracks. Some of them play nice while we’re watching, and differently while we’re not. And we can’t even check what their priorities are. That’s the state of my scientific field right now, sadly.

And the plan—and yes, I think this is what happens if we do nothing—is to make these untrustworthy AIs smarter than us, have them improve themselves as fast as possible to a potentially uncontrollable level of intelligence, copy them billions of times, and hook them up to run our economies, control our weapons, and advise our leaders. I mean, what are we thinking?


If we train a billion genius traitors and give them control of the most powerful instruments of society, there won’t be an America. There won’t be a China. There won’t be an India anymore… because we’ll all be dead.

If society weren’t integrating AI so aggressively, I’d have had to explain how these systems would forcefully integrate themselves.

Call them “traitors,” not “schemers”

I think “traitor” is accurate and more approachable, with bonus points for the conference’s military / geopolitical focus. Min-i-mize jargon!

Call out big-money interests

Some big money interests want you to believe that even the tiniest bit of caution will ruin your country. Think about it this way. Big tobacco lied about lung cancer. Big oil lied about climate change. And now parts of big AI say these risks are fake. Science fiction. Right. They advocate putting these currently untrustworthy machines into the most important parts of our economy, have them advise our leaders, have them run our most powerful weapons. What could go wrong? Science fiction.

Some big AI investors promote narratives that whistleblowers like me are secretly in the pocket of big AI, that the fear is just hype.

As an aside, Andrew Ng spoke the day before me. Andrew has also invested big in AI. Andrew has also been impressively wrong. He thought real AI would be hundreds or thousands of years away, which seems tenuous:

The case against killer robots, from a guy actually working on artificial intelligence (2015)

“I don’t work on preventing AI from turning evil for the same reason that I don’t work on combating overpopulation on the planet Mars,” he said. “Hundreds of years from now when hopefully we’ve colonized Mars, overpopulation might be a serious problem and we’ll have to deal with it. It’ll be a pressing issue. There’s tons of pollution and people are dying and so you might say, ‘How can you not care about all these people dying of pollution on Mars?’ Well, it’s just not productive to work on that right now.”

Current AI systems, Ng contends, are basic relative to human intelligence, even if there are things they can do that exceed the capabilities of any human. “Maybe hundreds of years from now, maybe thousands of years from now—I don’t know—maybe there will be some AI that turn evil,” he said, “but that’s just so far away that I don’t know how to productively work on that.”


Andrew Ng says AGI is decades away—and the real AI bubble risk is in the training layer (2026)

FastCompany: Agentic AI is rapidly increasing systems’ ability to reason and act with limited human intervention. Does the rise of agentic architectures meaningfully accelerate the path toward AGI, or are we still far from true general intelligence?

Andrew Ng: Most of the public thinks of AGI as AI that is as intelligent as people, and one useful definition is AI that can perform any intellectual task a human can. You and I could learn to fly an airplane with maybe 20 hours of training, learn to drive a truck through a forest, or spend a few years writing a PhD thesis. Most humans can do these things. We’re still very far from AI meeting that definition of AGI.

For alternative definitions that some businesses have put forward—definitions that dramatically lower the bar—you could argue we already achieved AGI. There’s a good chance that under these lower-bar definitions, some businesses will soon try to declare success. But that won’t mean AI has reached human-level intelligence—it will simply mean the definition has been reworked to fit a much lower threshold.

Maybe a year ago, AGI felt 50 years away. Over the past year, perhaps we’ve made a solid 2% of progress, with another 49 years to go. These numbers are metaphorical, so don’t take them too seriously. [Laughs] But we are closer than before, yet many decades away from an AI that matches human intelligence. If you stick with the original definition—aligned with what people genuinely imagine AGI to be—we remain very, very far away.

In 2015, he said that worrying about evil AI is like worrying about “overpopulation on the planet Mars”:

AI guru Ng: Fearing a rise of killer robots is like worrying about overpopulation on Mars (2015)

“There’s also a lot of hype, that AI will create evil robots with super-intelligence. That’s an unnecessary distraction,” Ng told techies gathered at Nvidia’s GPU Technology Conference in San Jose, California, on Thursday.

“Those of us on the frontline shipping code, we’re excited by AI, but we don’t see a realistic path for our software to become sentient.

“There’s a big difference between intelligence and sentience. There could be a race of killer robots in the far future, but I don’t work on not turning AI evil today for the same reason I don’t worry about the problem of overpopulation on the planet Mars.

“If we colonize Mars, there could be too many people there, which would be a serious pressing issue. But there’s no point working on it right now, and that’s why I can’t productively work on not turning AI evil.”

In person, I gently asked him about this viewpoint. He told me he hasn’t changed his mind. I then asked, “don’t you think we’ve set foot on the planet?”, but he said “no.” He declined to discuss the matter further.

item.title: Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety” by Miles Brundage
item.description:
This reading was previously included Day 2 of the BlueDot Governance course. In the newest version of the BlueDot Governance course, this reading is now optional. I was sad to see this reading removed because I think it’s a great provocation. However, since it’s no longer part of the core curriculum content, I’m publishing my notes separately from the rest of my day 2 notes.

A short extract:

Miles argues that: “At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)“:

Pre-call content:

At risk of taking you down a rabbit hole, I’ll add some context on this reading. Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry.

One of the most natural questions to ask is, “Why does Miles believe that we have so little time?” Fortunately, he links to a post that answers this question called Time’s Up for AI Policy (written Dec 2024). He writes:

AI that exceeds human performance in nearly every cognitive domain is almost certain to be built and deployed in the next few years.

The announcement of o3 today makes clear that superhuman coding and math are coming much sooner than many expected, and we have barely begun to think through or prepare for the implications of this


This post links to a Tweet of his around the same time (we can also see his retrospective take from March this year):

I’ll reshare some of my notes on maths progress here:

OpenAI has reported solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, which would be remarkably above trend if confirmed (there’s a dispute over whether someone else’s work made its way into the training data). However, it feels fair to say that the writing is on the wall (the mathematical community seems to agree, though there are a variety of perspectives on whether we’ll automate the components of a mathematicians job other than just producing proofs and how long that might take). They dropped 372 other results onto the internet and a few days ago, they dropped a few more results.

Aside: Miles has a bet with Gary Marcus on AI progress. In July, Metaculus assigned Gary a 90% chance of winning, but more recently it dropped to 30%.

I’ll share some additional alternate perspectives after the call, but for now I’ll share a quote from Richard Ngo:

I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread

I also have no doubt Eliezer Yudkowsky would be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing:

When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get.

.. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from.

Post-call content:

One reason why we might reject triage mode is if we broadly think AI progress is slower than folks at the labs think. We’ve already discussed this, but here’s two more considerations.

  • Dwarkesh Patel has argued that timelines are longer than many folk expect because of a lack of continual learning and poor sample efficiency.
  • Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL. He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling).

Towards the end of 2024, Steve Newman offered another possibility: what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we only become aware of the limitations of models over time?:

  • “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.”
  • “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.”

Here’s a few other reasons why we might reject it:

  • Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines, namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive. I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines (I'd be curious to know whether the researchers listed below still have such broad distributions).
  • Eliezer Yudkowsky appears to agree with Toby: “I make less pretense of knowing exact AI timelines than some. History shows that, while some scientists have correctly called where a tech trajectory will converge, whether later or sooner, there are almost no cases of anyone proclaiming a year and being correct.” Additionally he says: “I looked at “AI 2027” as a title and shook my head about how that was sacrificing credibility come 2027 on the altar of pretending to be a prophet and picking up some short-term gains at the expense of more cooperative actors. I didn’t bother pushing back because I didn’t expect that to have any effect. I have been yelling at people to shut up about trading their stupid little timelines as if they were astrological signs for as long as that’s been a practice (it has now been replaced by trading made-up numbers for p(doom)).”
  • Christoph Winter and Charlie Bullock propose “radical optionality” as a strategy for navigating the possibility of transformative AI possibly arriving soon (in the next 10 years) on the basis of us having profound uncertainty over how this will develop and what policy responses are necessary. The term ‘radical’ is operative—unlike other more common, moderate optionality proposals they advocate investing extraordinary amounts of resources (this reading is now in day 3 of the governance course)
