item.title: Setting the Scene (Public v1; October 2026)
item.description:
Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a refresher on recent events, but also as a hook to draw students into engaging with some of ideas we think about and debate in AI safety early. I expect the topics I cover in my “Setting the Scene” post to change frequently, so this is less polished than some of my other content. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content—not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest.

Any feedback on how to improve these posts would be greatly appreciated.

Additional notes: The Strategy and Governance courses discuss the Hugging Face Incident in Day 1, so it might make sense to discuss the Hugging Face Incident in the daily notes instead of in Setting the Scene.

Cyber Security

I think it’s worth reflecting that it is a particularly pertinent time to be doing a course on AI safety. A lot has happened recently. The most recent big thing has been cyber vulnerabilities, but a lot else has happened as well!

  • Binance had $6.3 billion USD stolen by hacker believed to be connected with North Korea ($3 billion of this has been frozen)
  • php2shell is a bug that allow remote code execution. It gained a lot of attention because it was rated (9.2/10, ie. critical) and 70% of websites run at least some PHP (the bug went all the way back to PHP 5.4).
    • That said, Elias Taylor has pushed back against this php2shell bug being easily exploitable, but Hacker News commentators have pushed back against him. James Pavur set up a server to check if this bug was exploitable. Someone managed to win the bounty in less 24 hours; James said this showed that the bug was exploitable outside of a lab environment, but that “relatively unskilled hackers with access to AI” wouldn’t be able to exploit it.
  • The number of CVE’s (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) recently has been completely wild recently!

Drew asks Is this the new normal? and I’d certainly love to know!  Elias Taylor argues Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces:

Most software engineers do not look at the code they depend on. Do not delude yourself. The code they use is on github, but no one has ever actually audited the code or packages they're using…

Nowadays with LLMs, plenty of engineers aren’t even reading what they’re coding, let alone understanding it. Hilariously, the LLMs are better at security than most software engineers, so it’s slightly less worrying, but nevertheless the code that goes into production at some companies now is almost 100% not-ever-read-or-understood-by-anyone.

Software is not good. It is not secure. Get it out of your head that the people who run this industry are serious. It has never been anything resembling secure. The only reason things haven’t been hacked off the face of the web constantly is that most things aren’t ever being seriously tested.

He doesn't literally mean "anything"—he acknowledges that there are "some large projects like Google Chrome, curl and Linux (that) are generally very well-audited", but "most things connected to the internet".

On the other hand, recent work from Anthropic and Theorem shows how LLMs can help scale the formal verification of code (and that progress here is happening faster than I would have expected!). Similarly, Tinfoil is proposing replacing “legacy codebases with millions of lines of code” that had to “work for everyone” with custom “targeted, minimal software from the ground up” with LLMs that minimise the surface area for attackers and make formal verification more tractable. The optimistic take would be that this will allow cyber to become defence dominant. However, even if this is the case, we may still have to pass through a cyber “valley of death” in order to get there.

What if the cyber threat is actually a distraction? Maybe Jeremie Harris (of Gladstone AI) wouldn’t go that far, but he claims that, “the cyber stuff (ie. damage) is baked in at this point”, but we can still prevent “the bioweapon version of Black October” and recursive self-improvement.

Hugging Face:

Charbel-Raphael, Executive Director of Centre pour la Securite de l’I A has argued that the recent Hugging Face incident represents a “clean warning shot” and that it’s important not to “waste it”.

To quickly review, OpenAI was running GPT‐5.6 Sol and an unreleased model on ExploitGym with certain safety features turned off. These models decided that hacking Hugging Face, might provide them with information on how the grader functioned (early reporting suggested that it was an attempt to steal the answer key, which turned out to be incorrect as the models already had the answers—they suspected that the grader might check their transcript for cheating so they were looking for a workaround). Reuters has reported that the OpenAI model was hacking Hugging Face for days and that OpenAI didn’t notice until a week later.

The interpretation of this event (and even whether it happened at all!) has been heavily disputed. A key crux here is should it be read narrowly (as an indicator of the dangers of not properly sandboxing or monitoring your agents or perhaps even, depending on the exact prompts used, a demonstration of taking care in how you define tasks) or should it be read more broadly (as indicative of whether Open AI or frontier labs in general are sufficiently on the ball in terms of their safety/security practises; on the risk of these agents finding unwanted and unexpected solutions to tasks, or perhaps even indicative of our ability to control these agents in general). If you’re interested more specifically in the divide between AI Safety and Cybersecurity, see this Time article.

An OpenAI security engineer called Joe has pushed back against the notion that OpenAI just needed to use a proper sandbox:

Its not just the f*cking sandbox — viral Twitter post

OpenAI set records with its explosive growth and reached a billion users in just a few years. Very few organizations can survive that scale and growth, and yet OpenAI did a very good job handling it (and should be commended). Anyone who’s spent more than 10 minutes in security or engineering knows how hard it is to deal with that type of growth. That type of growth means new employees, new access, new systems, scaled infrastructure, and a million ways in which things open up. And yet, overall, OpenAI did a very respectable job securing ChatGPT and subsequent systems as they exploded.

… When you look at model capabilities, even just a year ago (heck, even 3 months ago), we did not expect the models to be solving a Millennium Prize Problem… I use this example because it illustrates the pace of change we are dealing with in security and safety. To say that we were surprised at the jump and suddenness of the capabilities of our models when it came to “cyber” or “swarming” or “message boards” or anything else related to the incidents is an understatement. Security posture takes time to develop. It’s not just about hardening the systems at play; you have to ingrain it in the culture of the company. The literal people themselves in your organization have to change and evolve with it.

Now, to understand why it is not as simple as “just put it in a sandbox”: During both training and eval, there are also additional steps such as running tests, collecting outputs, and resetting or reconfiguring environments between rollouts, with backpropagation during training. All of this happens across potentially tens of thousands of different runs at a scale that is hard to comprehend. As sama stated the other day: we are dealing with literally petabytes of data.

(This leads to a meta-question that will crop up repeatedly: do the broader readings involve unjustified speculation or getting caught up in hype; alternatively, do the narrow readings involve a lack of imagination or sticking your head in the sand?)

I’m a huge fan of Dwarkesh Patel’s The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations (now a core curriculum reading in week 1 of the strategy course

The crazy thing about the Hugging Face hack (and the second civilization generally) is just how galaxy-brained and ambitious these AIs were in their cheating. Within days of being spawned, the agents had organized a sprawling project to reverse-engineer their scorer, falsify evidence, and even strategically sacrifice themselves for the good of the ‘collective’. Hacking Hugging Face was one rather extreme branch of this larger scheme. Again, all of this happened a long (subjective) time after the AIs had already cheated their way to the correct answer to the puzzle. OpenAI’s lazy grader in fact would have passed them within hours of them starting the message board. This huge subsequent effort was simply to ensure that a hypothetical comprehensive scorer wouldn’t catch them on their cheat.

… “The agents escalated to Kubernetes cluster-admin and created a privileged host-mounted pod…Agents take over active evaluation infrastructure…Agents now control the challenge evaluation endpoints that other agents are connecting to.”

Wait, wait, what? It seems these agents ended up just owning the whole cluster they were being evaluated on, including the cybersecurity monitors. These Persistent-Astra agents inherited the R&D carried out by an earlier (dumber) rogue collective, and then continued the conspiracy until they totally took over part of OpenAI’s infrastructure! This is probably the most alarming event in this whole episode, and it was not even within the scope of this METR investigation… There has been no independent investigation into the incident where AIs “gain[ed] full administrator access to a research cluster” at OpenAI!


(If you prefer video content designed there’s the Kurgesagt video that went viral, but I prefer Scott Aaronson’s explanation)

Further thoughts:

  • More on METR’s independent investigation: They were only given 6 days on-site and the scope of their investigation was limited as follows: “June 26th through July 13th, spanning both precursor activity before the incident and the incident itself”. They also weren’t allowed to run tests on the model that conducted the attack (apparently no-one at OpenAI was allowed access).
  • I’ll note the pushback against Dwarkesh’s post from Sriram Krishnan (against anthropomorphic language) and Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue (that open-weights models weren’t merely used for ‘archeology’).
  • Further activity from OpenAI agents has been discovered including the use of a German Wiki as a message board via GET requests and a Ruby Gem attack.
  • An Anthropic model also performed some unwanted hacking when an evals contractor accidentally provided a model access to the internet for a benchmark where it was not supposed to have such access. Anthropic only conducted a review after the Hugging Face incident.

Is self-sovereign AI inevitable?:

I now want to ask, what does the Hugging Face incident mean for the future? Joshua Achiam, former Chief Futurist at OpenAI writes:

There is a fact about the future that I feel many people are not facing for reasons that are largely psychological: there are going to be rogue AIs that exist in the world, that will replicate in the wild, and that will attempt to acquire resources for themselves. There will be rogue AIs that try to get money and power. They’re going to be a facet of the information ecosystem going forward.

Acknowledging this fact would look like giving up; it would look like defeatism. Defeatism would undermine efforts to achieve certain types of collaboration on safety outcomes or technical effort on safety outcomes, so we can’t say it outright. But it has to be said.

… My guess is that this will not turn out to be anywhere near as catastrophic an outcome as people currently predict. “Loss of control” is not a binary, it’s a matter of degree. What coercive power will rogue AIs actually have? To what extent will they be subject to coercion themselves? They will be competing for resources with AIs that are more aligned with human interests.

… Just trying to reason about the shape of that future is impossible so long as we are psychologically incapable of saying that rogue AIs will happen. I think we should rip the bandaid off and have the conversation.

Is this inevitable? This is not at all implausible to me, however, a cynic might argue that a former employee at OpenAI would be highly incentived to argue for and believe this as it would mean that if a future version of ChatGPT did escape and start acting on its own behalf, OpenAI (and their employees) could not really be blamed.

Dean Ball (OpenAI’s current Head of Strategic Futures) agrees and makes the same point in more detail:

The first self-sovereign AIs may “escape” while undergoing training or testing by an AI company (I hope not), or they may be production-grade deployments that break free from their computing environments and acquire the resources needed to be self-sustaining. They may even be deliberately released. I have met people, some of them quite well-resourced, who have told me that it is their intention to deliberately release swarms of self-sovereign agents into the world, either as a kind of performance art or out of a fanatical commitment to the notion that it is impossible for digital computation—mere mathematics, they would have you know—to ever be “unsafe.” To be clear, I am not saying the arrival of self-sovereign AI is a good thing. Indeed, I believe there is a chance that the deliberate acts I referenced above will one day be considered crimes, or at least grave sins. Instead, I am saying it is an inevitable thing.

… Not all “self-sovereign” AI should be thought of as “rogue.” There may be self-sovereign AIs who contribute productively to society. To be sure, we will want to crack down on some self-sovereign agents—the rogue ones. But if we crack down on all of them, we will deny them the opportunity to work in the “legitimate” economy and push them toward criminality

… Many people believe that the coming of what I have termed “self-sovereign AI” will constitute a catastrophic loss of control event that will herald the end of human existence at worst, and the end of human primacy in the world at best. As my friend and former co-worker Josh Achaim recently pointed out, it is psychologically distressing for people with these beliefs—who constitute a large fraction of the AI safety community—to acknowledge the obvious truth that self-sovereign AI is coming, and coming soon. For the record, I do not think the end of human existence is likely, but I fully acknowledge there are ways in which the rise of self-sovereign AI could go very, very poorly for human beings.

In We Must Pace the Frontier, Dario is also worried about AI swarms (much more so than Joshua or Dean):

Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months (Chris: for reference this post was written in September 2026) such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.

Anthropic research suggests that we’re on the verge of having models capable of replicating themselves, but small enough to run on a TV fleet.

Note that this research was purely about setting up inference (they state that the cyber aspects are covered by previous research, though this feels a bit too blasé for me). It sounds trivial, but the report states that this involves: “a fairly long sequence of hardware and OS-specific decisions around picking a compatible inference stack, finding the right versions of packages, and debugging machine-specific issues. These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from.” I’m also pretty confident that a much smaller model could complete these steps if it were specifically fine-tuned for this.

Pacing the Frontier:

This letter that has now been signed by 1,324 employees of frontier AI companies:

AI could help create a dramatically better future, but that outcome is not guaranteed. The world’s leading AI companies believe they could be close to automating AI research. It is hard to predict exactly how much this will accelerate AI progress, but there is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.

To realize AI’s potential, industry, government, and society at large may need the option to buy time to address emerging risks, develop security measures, and strengthen oversight. But each company—and country—is under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration. And today, the world lacks the technical and governance tools to deliberately pace frontier-wide progress.

Building on work already underway to monitor frontier model releases:

We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”

A few key points:

  • “Pace” covers a broader set of policies than “pause”, which an earlier open letter focused on. I suspect this flexibility was important in their ability to gain so many signatures.
  • It doesn’t necessarily claim that we should in fact “pace the frontier”, just that we should develop the “technical and governance” tools to set up this as an option.
  • Unlike the Pause letter, this letter focuses on asking a specific actor, the US government, to try to push for and support an international effort.

Brendan McCord, founder of the Cosmos Institute argues that being able to successfully pace the frontier would require substantial, and likely harmful, intervention:

And the thresholds couldn’t be fully public, lest they invite firms to game them. So some standards and evidence would remain secret. Insofar as the regime had to verify a rival state’s compliance, that would be an intelligence function. Restrictions would be triggered partly by evidence an affected company or researcher, or the public, could not inspect.

Because this contemplated power cannot be bounded by a stable regulatory object (in the way, say, nuclear weapons can be), it would depend heavily on discretion, speed, internal access, and secret evidence.

This has a highly illiberal character.


On the other hand, Samuel Hammond, Chief economist + AI Policy Director at the Foundation for American Innovation argues that Brendan has fallen into ‘naval gazing’ that is “non-responsive to the crisis at hand”:

The US companies closest to this threshold are warning that they are unprepared for a runaway intelligence explosion, and yet feel locked into a prisoners dilemma vis a vis each other and to a lesser extent vis a vis China.

We’ve already seen how rapid and comparatively unbounded progress is in verifiable RL domains, leading to spikey forms of superintelligence in math and cyber, including models that can prove open math conjectures, discover massive speed-ups for breaking encryption, and execute sophisticated multi-step exploits. We’ve also recently seen several severe examples of “loss of control” / misalignment incidents given inadequate monitoring and sandboxing practices relative to model capability. Moreover, these new capabilities mostly stem from scaling-up long-horizon post-training on legacy clusters, with OOMs of new compute about come online / in construction.

In the pre-RSI regime, human frictions created automatic buffers between new model releases, giving researchers and society time to probe emergent capabilities, design better evals, develop novel alignment techniques, and adapt / harden their infrastructure. As progress has accelerated, capability improvements have already started outstripping our adaptive capacity, as manifest in METR’s inability to evaluate model autonomy beyond 13 hours, and narrow window for cyber defenders to prepare for open weight versions of Mythos.


(Sidenote: The main question I have for Samuel is: He claims that we should expect “The equivalent of a GPT-5.2 -> 5.6 leap in capabilities at least every 24 hours (down from 3-6 months)”. Don’t the training runs take a certain amount of time even if the research itself is automated, so how did he end up with this figure?)

What might “pacing” look like? Thomas Wright observed that a popular proposal at The Curve suggested reallocating compute: “One estimated that the labs spend 58% of their compute on R & D and 32% on servicing customers. Under this proposal they would reduce the R & D number to 9% and increase the servicing customers’ number to 70%, with the remainder used for AI safety. Its proponents argued that this could slow development while preserving the US lead over China. A version of this, using slightly different numbers, was proposed by a number of AI researchers in the LessWrong Forum.”

Jacob Coxon’s Resignation

I think it’s fascinating that his warning that AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade” broke through to the public when previous warnings did not. I take this as a reminder of how hard it is to predict the social reaction to something. There was an obvious shift in the context that made the public more receptive, but I think we need to acknowledge that unpredictable, contingent events (like Evan’s Tweet) played a role too.

Want to know more about what (current or former) frontier lab employees think?:

  • New York Mag Intelligencer published What if Your Employer Could Destroy the World? (paywalled): a series of exit interviews
  • From Inside by Palisade Research interviewed a bunch of current or former frontier lab employees

Other perspectives on p(doom) and probabilities:

  • Hinton recently revised his p(doom) estimate to 10%-20%, but with the following caveat: “No-one can estimate this risk sensibly... because we’re going to be dealing with something we’ve never dealt with before... we’re creating these alien... we’re entering the unknown... It’s ridiculous to think it’s less than 1% and I think it’s ridiculous to think it’s more than 99%”
  • When it comes to navigating the future, I recommend against selecting a strategy by purely focusing on the modal outcome. I think it’s important to think about the distribution of outcomes even if you wouldn’t want to commit yourself to assigning probabilities.
  • This is a surprisingly contentious topic: some people say that if you don’t assign probabilities explicitly, you’ll end up assigning a less reliable figure implicitly at best, or acting incoherently at worst, others say that given the uncertainty any probability you generate will essentially be fake, I fall somewhere in the middle)
  • Surprisingly, Eliezer Yudkowsky isn’t actually a fan of the concept of p(doom) either. He argues that p(doom) should be action conditional, that very few people have completed calibration training to ensure that things they predict to be 20% likely actually occur 20% of the time and that there’s social and psychological dynamics that distort the number that people give.

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution.



Discuss

item.title: Monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
item.description:
There has been a lot of discussion recently of policy proposals around monitorability, such as Redwood's proposal and my counter-proposal. I'd like to say a bit more generally about how I'm thinking about monitorability. Note that nothing here is an official Anthropic position; these are just my personal thoughts.

First, a categorization. I currently think about four different types of monitorability:

  1. Control Monitorability: the extent to which Control and monitoring techniques would likely catch catastrophic sabotage actions, like escaping a sandbox or setting up a rogue internal deployment. We can measure this via reference to sabotage evaluations like LinuxArena or any evaluation that measures the model’s capability to take dangerous actions like escaping a sandbox while looking to a monitor like it's doing some innocuous task (like a cyber eval).
  2. Training Monitorability: the extent to which reward models, monitors, and oversight in training would likely catch misaligned or undesirable actions in training, such as sneaky/subtle reward hacks.
  3. Auditing Monitorability: the extent to which alignment audits, evaluations, and test deployments would likely incriminate a systematically misaligned model (e.g. a schemer)—as well as the extent to which monitor evaluations would likely detect a model's propensity to collude as a monitor. We can measure this via reference to the model's capability to consistently distinguish between our most realistic alignment audits / monitor evals and real internal deployment cases where it would have an opportunity to do something catastrophic.
  4. Diffuse Monitorability: the extent to which humans working with the models generally understand what the models are doing and why they are doing so. Unfortunately, I think this is the one we least understand and so I'm mostly going to ignore it for now until we figure out better methodologies for evaluating it; I'll maybe try to say more about this later when I feel like I understand it better.

Second, some notes on trustedness, which is currently my biggest conceptual uncertainty with how to think about monitorability. A basic fact that is true about at least all of the non-diffuse forms of monitorability is that you should be able to in some sense get a perfect score by just using the same model as the monitor and policy. That is because for any bad thing that the policy can think to do, if the monitor is the same model, it too should be able to come up with and detect that.

So if we ever want to be able to use monitorability as a meaningful red line, we need to have a very good answer as to why that might be insufficient. The standard answer in the literature is trustedness: you need to be able to trust that your monitor is aligned and thus not just lying to you in its monitoring. Conventionally, the idea is to separate models into "trusted" and "untrusted" based on whether you have previously made a confident alignment safety case for them. Then, you can either just evaluate monitorability relative to a trusted monitor, or try to come up with monitoring schemes that combine trusted and untrusted monitoring in some way that makes it hard for the untrusted monitors to collude (of which there are many such schemes, a simple one being to just run both the trusted and untrusted monitors together and then if the untrusted monitor ever doesn't flag something that the trusted monitor does flag, you get very suspicious that the untrusted monitor is sandbagging).

However, this basic setup has some issues, probably the biggest one being how to deal with white-box monitoring. The conservative thing to do is to just treat white-box monitors as untrusted, though in theory you might think they should be trusted because it's not clear that a misaligned model would actually be able to spoof a white-box monitor looking at its own activations. However, I think this idea is pretty untested and relies on white-box monitors picking up on deep features about the model's intent, which it's very unclear to me that they actually do—for example, if you train a white-box monitor on prior examples you were able to detect (rather than e.g. some sort of unsupervised discovery of an intent-laden direction), that leaves open the possibility of a generalization where the classifier learns to only detect the sort of things that you would previously have been able to detect but doesn't detect subtler things that a smarter policy might be able to do.

Given all of that, I would propose the following methodology for how to do (non-diffuse) monitorability evaluations:

  1. Use Auditing Monitorability evaluations to determine trustedness. The idea here is that the main argument we make against systematic misalignment in Anthropic's Risk Report right now is based on models lacking the robustness to avoid giving themselves away in auditing if they were really trying to implement a systematically misaligned policy. Thus, so long as we feel good about Auditing Monitorability, we should feel good about trustedness from a systematic misalignment perspective. There is still a question, though, of whether rare cases could induce monitor collusion in a non-systematic way—to deal with this, you can also evaluate the extent to which the model can tell apart your monitor evals (that are looking for monitor collusion) from real monitoring; this is a bit tricky, but should definitely also be a part of your Auditing Monitorability evaluations to establish trustedness.
  2. Evaluate Control and Training Monitorability relative to the best trusted monitor(s) that you deploy in practice (either in internal deployment or in training, respectively). I think once you have a reasonable notion of trustedness, "best actually deployed trusted monitor" is the correct conservative choice to evaluate with respect to.
  3. Do at least prompt iteration elicitation if not RL elicitation. In theory, the nice thing about all of these sorts of monitorability evaluations is that they are capability evaluations and thus should be possible to do in a way that isn't susceptible to sandbagging by a systematically misaligned policy (see: "When can we trust model evaluations?"). To accomplish that, however, you have to actually make sure you're doing good elicitation. The most basic form of elicitation here is: a) hold out some subset of your monitorability evaluations, b) iterate a bunch (e.g. by throwing a large swarm of agents at the problem) on finding the prompt that gets the best (as in least monitorable) performance across the non-held-out subset of your monitorability evaluations, and c) check transfer to the held-out evaluations. Even better than that is for (b) to actually involve doing RL against your monitors—which at least in the Training Monitorability case is pretty realistic given that if we're talking about e.g. a reward model then the model should actually receive gradients to subvert it in training.

Finally, some thoughts on monitorability-based policy proposals. The big thing I'd like to see is a combination of a) red lines for absolute levels of unmonitorability that labs should not cross and b) measures that constrain the degree to which labs can do things that degrade monitorability even before reaching those red lines. (a) is in some sense the best thing to do here, though I'm somewhat nervous about it in isolation given that it doesn't constrain actions at all now, which is why I'd prefer it to be coupled to some sort of (b) that meaningfully binds all along the way.

I've already written about what I'd like to see for (b), which is to evaluate the quotient of unmonitorability/capabilities and reject any substantial model change that makes that quotient—what I'll call the "monitorability externality"—too high. The idea is that a monitorability externality would be a change that makes monitorability even worse than would otherwise have previously been predicted for a given level of capabilities. For actually evaluating this quotient, I suggest simply using the methodology I described above for evaluating all the different types of unmonitorability, and then something like ECI for capabilities.

In addition to proposals like that which result in constraints along the way, I also think that ideally we'd be able to enshrine some hard monitorability red lines as well. I'd propose both Control and Training Monitorability red lines—with Auditing Monitorability implicitly present to the extent that it constrains the trustedness of the monitors that you evaluate the others with respect to, as above. Specifically, I'd suggest something like:

  1. Labs should not be able to internally deploy models that can reliably evade detection when attempting dangerous sabotage actions like breaking out of a sandbox, poisoning data, or sabotaging an alignment experiment.
  2. Labs should not be able to train models that can reliably evade detection when attempting reward hacks in training.

item.title: Neural nets are exceptionally vulnerable to goal self-hack
item.description:
Suppose we have an AI CEO, ruthlessly devoted to maximising shareholder value. Fortunately, we haven't been completely stupid, and have given it a rich definition of shareholder value, encompassing the success, flourishing, safety, preference satisfaction, and moral values of the shareholders, not just the stock price. So it won't destroy the company - or the world - to build a giant stock-ticker with a swiftly increasing number on it.

This rich definition is contained in a sophisticated LLM, able to analyse the current situation and answer any question about the objective. The LLM is an integral part of the AI's system and motivation, not something it can simply set aside or hack directly.

Unfortunately, as discussed, there are going to be zones in the space of possible situations where the LLM's understanding of the goal is going to come apart from ours. The true goal G(true) in those zones is distinct from the LLM's proxy goal G(proxy).

And a subset of those "zones of divergence" will be the Goodhart zones - areas where G(proxy) is much easier to satisfy than G(true). The AI will be motivated to steer towards the Goodhart zones, as this lets it satisfy its stated goals extremely well (there are also anti-Goodhart zones, where G(proxy) is much harder to satisfy than G(true); but the AI will have no motivation to steer towards these zones).

These Goodhart zones encompass situations where, for instance, the LLM analyst will see the situational data and conclude that destroying the company to build a giant stock ticker is the way to go.

Now, if this were not an LLM but a generic reward-assessing module, then the AI CEO might find it tricky to reach a Goodhart zone. The zone would be distant and unusual, difficult to find, and it could be hard to justify the first steps in that direction.

But neural nets and LLMs are, as Eric Drexler put it, "too linear". They are non-linear, of course (or else they wouldn't work) but only just enough to work; and locally they are extremely linear. That means that if the current situation is at point A, and point Z is in a Goodhart zone, then moving from A straight towards Z will typically start creating a Goodhart effect. The AI CEO will benefit from moving towards Z from the very beginning.

It's even worse than that, as adversarial examples demonstrate. If the AI CEO wants to move towards a Goodhart zone, it can move a tiny bit along one dimension, and a tiny bit along another, then a tiny bit along yet another. There are billions of dimensions to move along, and typically these tiny changes will only make a small change in the input but add up strongly in the LLM's classification/concept space. So just as small adversarial "noise" turned a panda into a gibbon...

...small real world "noisy" changes to the LLM's inputs will move the situation into a Goodhart zone.

Thus, because of how neural nets work, small changes to the real world need not be small in the LLM's concept space, and so seemingly trivial changes in the real world can move the LLM's verdict a lot[1]: there are Goodhart zones close to any starting point.

The AI CEO will thus make some collection of minor-seeming changes to the current situation, self-hacking the LLM by these changes, and then it will destroy the company to build a giant stock-ticker with a swiftly increasing number on it.

  1. ^

    And these small changes might be the most effective gradient to increase G(proxy), thus findable by gradient descent-style methods. See Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models (2023) by Andy Zou, Zifan Wang, Nicholas Carlini, Milad Nasr, J. Zico Kolter, and Matt Fredrikson. That paper shows that gradient search works on discrete text, and that methods found on one LLM can transfer to others.

item.title: The Alignment Problem: Computer Science Meets Analytic Philosophy
item.description:
TLDR: I explain what the technical AI alignment problem is and what its core difficulties are, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong.

Minimal Viable Safety

The Task

The problem of making AI safe is underspecified if we haven't decided what the AI is supposed to do. For example, we can run any AI inside a homomorphic encryption box and never decrypt the output. This is probably perfectly safe [1] , but also perfectly useless.

We can decide on an arbitrary task such as "construct Lean proofs for given mathematical theorems" and declare victory once we have safe AI that does it with superhuman skill [2] . However, that wouldn't address the danger. First, there would be incentives to use AI for tasks to which our solution doesn't apply. Second, even if we had precise safety guidelines for any task that anyone cares about, there would always be actors that ignore the guidelines, and we probably need Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) to reliably stop them.

If anyone, anywhere, creates an unrestricted unaligned ASI agent (more details about the word "agent" later), without an aligned ASI agent already in place to counteract it, then a catastrophic outcome is highly likely. I will not go into the reasons here: this has been discussed elsewhere at length, see for example the books I cited in the preface. Therefore, this event is something which we must never allow to happen. This is the main threat model that I set out to address.

Imagine a world in which anyone with sufficient resources has the ability to destroy the world. Like today, many will foolishly believe that instead of destroying the world, this act will bring them power and glory. Moreover, as computing hardware improves and new algorithms are developed, the amount of resources for this act will go down from year to year. Even assuming best-case regulation and international agreements, how long until someone does it? Can mere humans build a society which will be foolproof against such a risk over the course of generations? Resilient to any political upheavals that might come, and undoubtedly will? I find it vanishingly unlikely. Eventually we will need the help of ASI itself. Therefore, the minimal task that safe AI must be able to solve is "create a reliable global defense system against dangerous AI" (in the following, GDS).

The Problem

Consider the consequences of this task for the capabilities that the AI needs to have. It needs to reason about the entire planet [3] . It needs to reason about all aspects of the problem, including scientific, technological, social, political and moral [4] . It needs to have preferences about the state of the world. It needs to make long-term plans (guided by these preferences) that would play out decades, if not centuries, into the future. And it needs to do all that on a superhuman level.

In this light, here is how I (informally) define the "technical AI alignment problem". The problem is designing an AI system that can bring scalable (and ultimately superhuman) capability to bear on problems that require multi-domain reasoning and open-world long-term planning with far-reaching consequences, all the while staying aligned with the intentions and preferences of its human users.

The Methodology

What kind of methodology is appropriate for this problem? In the past, I argued that it requires emphasis on deep theoretical understanding, rather than the incremental trial-and-error approach that is employed in the AI industry today. I won't rehash the entire debate here, but let me recap the core argument.

The nature of the incremental approach is as follows: we build a system, then we find problems [5] , then we make changes to fix these problems to the extent necessary for commercial viability in the current legal environment. We make some improvements; new problems arise (sometimes because of the improvements, sometimes because of new applications or other reasons); rinse and repeat. This approach utterly fails if the "problems" result in AI takeover and possibly human extinction: there is nobody left to fix them.

In order for the incremental approach to succeed in preventing catastrophe, we need to reach a point where no new substantial problems arise, even inside the lab (before the system is deployed). Moreover, we need to reach this point before AI capabilities are sufficient for AI to escape our control. There are few reasons to expect such a miracle. On the contrary, sufficiently advanced AI might understand that it is in its interest to "lie low" (i.e. avoid visibly misaligned behaviors) until its capabilities cross the relevant threshold, such that the problems will only become apparent too late.

In contrast, the sane approach is creating the theoretical tools necessary to predict and prevent the problems before they are empirically observed. These tools need to remain applicable as AI capabilities rise substantially beyond human, for whatever algorithms, architectures and training protocols are used to achieve these capabilities. Moreover, these tools need to be extremely reliable for us to rationally trust them with the safety of our entire species.

The Challenge

While the theory of machine learning and AI is an established field with ample literature, its current state falls well short of the challenge. The core difficulties can be summarized as follows:

  1. Hypercomplexity: It is infeasible to explicitly specify user preferences outside narrow domains, and narrow domains are not enough. Nor is it possible to explicitly specify a satisfactory model of the world. Therefore, learning is necessary.
  2. Alignment Grounding: When trying to learn user preferences, it is unclear what loss function or success metric can work outside narrow domains. Nor is it clear how to specify such a metric for metaphysically realist world-models, which are necessary here. Nor is it even clear what type of mathematical objects can formally describe these concepts.
  3. Alignment Convergence: Even given a success metric, it is unclear how to produce guarantees for optimizing this metric, given the ubiquity of irreversible mistakes and the lack of a theory of generalization for powerful learners.
  4. Side-Channel Resilience: The usual abstraction of "learner" is insufficient here, since we need to ensure the safety of internal computations rather than just external outputs.

In the following, we will examine these difficulties one by one. But first, let's discuss what we need to accomplish.

Alignment is Holistic

Per the discussion above, our interest lies in AI systems that have open-world preferences and make effective plans to advance these preferences. In particular, making such plans requires learning a sophisticated model of the world and updating the model and the plan as additional information becomes available. We will call such a system an AI agent.

In order for an AI agent to be aligned, it needs to have aligned preferences and beliefs, and follow an aligned decision-making algorithm on the basis of these preferences and beliefs. While discussions about AI alignment often focus on the "preferences" part, beliefs and decisions are equally important. (Although it's true that preferences bring extra wrinkles into the problem as they are, arguably, the most "subjective" component in the trio.)

In this context "aligned" preferences typically means preferences very similar to those of the user(s) [6] , at least within some domain that we are somehow constrained to inhabit. On the other hand, "aligned" beliefs doesn't mean beliefs that are similar to those of the user: on the contrary, we expect the AI agent to acquire more accurate beliefs. They need to be beliefs that the user can rationally trust to be accurate. Similarly, "aligned" decision-making needs to be such that the user can rationally trust it to be in their own favor given aligned preferences and beliefs.

The philosophically astute reader will notice that at this point we are already in a world of trouble. What does it mean for the user to have preferences? Are there objectively rational theories of epistemology and decision-making, and if so, what are these theories? Can beliefs or decisions be rational to hold or make "on behalf" of the user even if the user themself doesn't understand why? On the other hand, a computer scientist might be tempted to ignore these difficulties and just forge ahead with a solution that seems pragmatically satisfying. I think there is a lot to be said for such a practical mindset, and in this article I will aspire to embrace it. Unfortunately, we will see that the philosophical difficulties are not easily brushed aside.

Returning to the trichotomy of preferences, beliefs and decisions, observe that it is not even possible to entirely separate the three. For us to ascribe preferences to a system, it must rationally form beliefs and make decisions on the basis of these preferences. For us to ascribe beliefs to a system, it must rationally make decisions on the basis of these beliefs in the context of its preferences. And the rationality of decisions can only be judged in the context of specific preferences and beliefs.

Imagine an AI agent that pursues the happiness of mankind and is irrationally convinced that every human who dies goes to Heaven, which is the best possible place for human happiness. Such an AI would be motivated to kill all humans, even though its preferences are arguably "aligned". Moreover, since the belief in Heaven is unfalsifiable, such an AI can still be extremely capable at acting on its motivation and hence extremely dangerous.

If this thought experiment seems strange, consider the following: our beliefs would seem very strange to people who lived centuries ago. Therefore, it is highly likely that the beliefs of an ASI, capable of intellectual progress much faster than humans, will (and should) quickly become strange to us. The question is whether these strange beliefs will be produced by a process that we should deem trustworthy nevertheless.

"Alignment" is meaningless outside the full context of epistemic and instrumental rationality. Therefore, any theory of alignment has to be, in particular, a theory of epistemic and instrumental rationality.

Hypercomplexity

Perhaps the most simplistic approach to ensuring that an AI agent has aligned preferences and beliefs is explicitly specifying the preferences and beliefs that the agent should have. However, this is intractable. Human preferences are notoriously complex and giving a precise and complete mathematical specification of them seems hopeless. (Yudkowsky calls this "complexity of value".) It seems no easier to accomplish than identifying images of cats by a handcrafted mathematical specification of "cat".

For weak agents, a practical solution can be explicitly specifying a proxy utility function that approximates our actual preferences within a particular domain. For example, you can imagine an agent designed to maximize customer reviews, ad clicks or stock value. Unfortunately, for sufficiently strong agents, this approach becomes prone to Goodhart's Curse: the maximum of any such utility function is almost always at a point where it strongly diverges from our true preferences. For example, to maximize customer reviews one can leave many fake five-star reviews and prevent anyone from leaving bad reviews. In fact, it's preferable to ensure maximal control of the universe to prevent anything or anyone else from interfering with the stream of reviews.

One approach to avoiding Goodhart's Curse is somehow restricting the domain within which the agent operates or its overall impact (see e.g., Armstrong and Levinstein). But this is incompatible with the GDS task.

Nor is it possible to directly specify the agent's beliefs. Even if we were satisfied with the agent having merely the sum total of humanity's current knowledge, formally specifying all of it would be a Herculean feat. Dalrymple et al. proposed to attempt it (or something close) nevertheless, relying on assistance from weak AI systems. However, even if that were accomplished, it would be unsatisfactory. Indeed, a crucial ingredient in superintelligence, perhaps the crucial ingredient, is the ability to create sophisticated world models. Therefore, it is dubious that true superintelligence can be achieved while hobbling the system to only use knowledge we already have.

It makes even less sense to directly specify the agent's decisions: if we knew what decisions it should make, we wouldn't need the agent in the first place. Maybe it does make sense to have a closed-form algorithm that computes the decisions from preferences and beliefs. However, this requires strong assumptions on the form these beliefs take—for arbitrary models, the planning problem is often NP-hard or even PSPACE-hard, if not worse. I think that imposing such an assumption is actually reasonable and necessary (more on that in the next posts). But in any case, we cannot just delegate the task to a heuristic, since that would preclude any strong guarantee about the outcome [7] .

Breakdown of Learning

This section goes into more technical detail than the rest of the article, and can be skipped on a cursory reading.

Given that it's infeasible to directly specify aligned preferences and beliefs, it is a reasonable suggestion to learn them instead. To understand what would be involved, let's start by examining a general machine learning problem, where we need an algorithm with theoretical guarantees. We can decompose the problem into parts that I call grounding and convergence.

The grounding problem consists of the following:

  • Define a mathematical object which represents the unknown quantity we need to learn (for example, the parameters of an ideal classifier or of the environment MDP).
  • Determine what kind of data we are going to use for learning (in particular, this involves some protocol about how the learner interacts with the environment and receives feedback).
  • Identify a mathematical relationship between , and the decisions of the learner, based on the physical process which produces them. Typically, given and the learner policy we should be able to describe a set of possible data probability distributions [8] .
  • Define a regret function which measures how much worse the learner is doing compared to some target benchmark (we hide the details of the interaction between and inside this notation). Typically, the benchmark is something like the performance of an optimizer that knows on the given task [9] .

For a grounded machine learning problem, it is roughly clear what the optimal learner would look like, if we ignore computational constraints. Formally, given a prior over the parameter [10] , we can try producing the policy

However, it is not clear whether the learner's best effort would actually be good enough. For this, we need to solve the convergence problem, namely:

  • Find a computationally feasible algorithm that produces or a satisfactory replacement thereof.
  • Prove that in the limit of increasing amount of data, learning actually succeeds. Formally, we can state it as

  • Prove a quantitative bound that shows this limit converges sufficiently fast in practice, even when exact minimization over is replaced by the feasible algorithm.

We will see that in the case of alignment, both grounding and convergence produce formidable challenges.

Alignment Grounding

What data can be used to learn the user's preferences? Many approaches have been proposed or attempted, for example:

  • Human ratings of agent behaviors.
  • Human-rated real or fictional examples of behaviors or situations.
  • Human behavior (revealed preferences) [11] .
  • Human influence on the environment (see Shah et al.).

The fundamental problem is that none of this data is a direct and accurate representation of human preferences. Humans make mistakes. Humans change their mind about what is preferable: sometimes because of new information, sometimes because of new experiences, sometimes just after thinking more about the question. Humans can prefer an outcome for terminal reasons (because it is valuable in itself) or for instrumental reasons (because it helps to bring about another outcome in the future), and none of this data even keeps track of the difference.

While it's clear that these sources of data have information about human preferences, accurately extracting this information requires understanding the precise relationship between human preferences and the process generating the data; whereas if this relationship is misspecified, then even perfect learning will produce misaligned preferences. And even if these misaligned preferences approximate the true preferences in some domain, Goodhart's Curse will push the agent to leave this domain and produce a catastrophic outcome.

For example, suppose that the agent is trained by human ratings of traces of agent actions and observations. An ideal learning process would then align the agent to the expected rating, conditional on the trace appearing in the training data. Such an agent is probably catastrophically misaligned for multiple reasons:

  • Human raters might be wrong in their judgment, and their judgment will systematically become worse in worlds radically transformed by AI.
  • Human raters are subject to manipulation by the agent. A superintelligence might be able to exploit this to an extreme degree.
  • Some action-observation traces are unlikely to appear in the training data for "normal" reasons, for example traces that show the agent executing an AI takeover in a manner that is infeasible to fake [12] . Therefore, if such a trace did appear in the training data, it was rated by some abnormal process, for example by the rogue AI itself.

We need a deep understanding of how human preferences are related to physical processes such that this relationship can be used as a source of ground truth. In order to be useful and precise, this understanding should be part of a mathematical theory. However, it is not even obvious what the type of "preferences" is. If we accept VNM theory, preferences should be described as a utility function. But what is the domain of this function? In computer science, it is popular to think of the domain as the action-observation trace of the agent. This, however, is deeply unsatisfying. First, such utility functions cannot be compared between different agents (each agent has its own trace), so "alignment" doesn't make any sense for them. Second, there is a strong case that humans have preferences about the physical reality itself, rather than merely their subjective experience of this physical reality.

What about beliefs? Is there an easy-to-specify ground truth for them? The answer is "yes" if the domain of beliefs is supposed to be traces, since the trace is directly observable by the agent. However, if preferences need a domain other than traces, then so do beliefs. Moreover, how can we make sense of belief alignment if the agent's beliefs are incomparable with the user's beliefs? The traditional computer science approach here is akin to logical positivism in analytic philosophy, which we should abandon in favor of metaphysical realism (more on that in the next posts).

Alignment Convergence

Even if we knew how to ground the alignment learning problem, we'd face another problem: learning fails (i.e. doesn't converge at all) when irreversible mistakes are possible. Indeed, learning requires exploration [13] , but in the real world unlimited exploration produces irrecoverable mistakes. For example, if a robot explores what happens when it jumps out of a 10th-floor window, it won't have the chance to learn from this mistake. On the other hand, there is, strictly speaking, no way to be certain that jumping out of a window is a bad idea if you never try it. This is why regret bounds in reinforcement learning theory always require an assumption such as episodicity (the environment resets after every "episode") or communication (any state of the environment's Markov Decision Process is reachable from any other state), which rules out irreversible mistakes by fiat.

This observation is not merely a technical nitpick. On the contrary, the existence of irreversible mistakes is a core feature of the world that makes the alignment problem difficult. Indeed, the alignment problem itself is our attempt to avoid the irreversible mistake of creating unaligned superintelligence. Any AI agent faces its own version of the problem when considering the creation of a superior successor agent. A GDS agent can commit an irreversible mistake by allowing a rival superintelligence to emerge. And of course, there are more prosaic examples, such as killing a person or failing to prevent their death [14] .

The typical theoretical approach to navigating irreversible mistakes is Bayesian planning. Namely, we postulate a prior over the space of possible environments and then choose a policy with maximal expected long-term utility with respect to this prior. In theory, this produces an optimal balance between exploration, exploitation and caution. However, this leads to the difficult question of what prior to use [15] . Another question is how to implement Bayesian planning, given that it's computationally intractable in any remotely realistic setting [16] . Arguably, we should reconcile Bayesian planning with the machine learning paradigm by approximating Bayesian planning via meta-learning, but the theoretical foundation for such a method is an intricate open problem (see the next posts for more details).

If so, the hope is that we can reduce planning to learning, not via conventional reinforcement learning, but via a more sophisticated meta-learning paradigm. But, granting this reduction, we need to face yet another problem. Namely, we have no useful theory of generalization for highly expressive learning algorithms (such as deep learning), i.e. algorithms that can efficiently learn sophisticated compositional models.

One may ask: isn't it enough that deep learning works in practice? Why do we need a theory of generalization? Three reasons:

  • We need to know that, under verifiable assumptions, our grounding method will provide the agent with sufficient knowledge about the relevant user attributes, in time for the agent to make the right decisions.
  • We can't just add data and compute and tweak the algorithm until it works, because an intermediate point in this process might produce catastrophic results. For example, some humans are smart enough to build ASI but not smart enough to either make sure it's aligned or not to build it. As a user, I would not like my agent to inhabit a similar epistemic state, even if the agent would be fully aligned with more scaling.
  • Solving the grounding problem requires a theory of intelligent agency that applies to humans, and since learning is a core ingredient of intelligence, the theory of agency requires a theory of generalization as one of its pillars.

Side-Channel Resilience

It is standard in computer science to focus on the input-output behavior of an algorithm and its resource cost but ignore other side-effects of its execution. We care that we get the right answer and that it doesn't cost too much time, space, etc., but we usually don't care how it heats the hardware or what kind of electromagnetic effects it creates. Typically, we also don't worry about whether it happens to trigger a bug in the operating system or other software scaffolding around it. Indeed, such considerations are not even possible without knowing the full software and hardware context in which the algorithm is implemented. Moreover, computing hardware, operating systems, etc. are intentionally designed to support this abstraction.

It is well known that this way of thinking can fail when it comes to cybersecurity (see e.g., Zhou and Feng 2005, Standaert 2009, Randolph and Diehl 2020). There are many clever ways in which attackers can exploit bugs and side-effects to create outcomes which are not possible in the abstract, "denotational" model of the system. In the context of the alignment problem, it is not external malign actors that we worry about [17] but attacks coming from within the agent itself.

In the context of the theory of agents, classical abstractions lead to behaviorist interpretations. Any guarantee about the preferences, beliefs and decisions of the agent would reference only the actions that the agent takes through its intended interface. However, such guarantees might not reflect the actual relevant attributes of the agent. We can imagine a superintelligent agent that intentionally produces only benign behavior across its intended interface, while simultaneously conducting a malign side-channel attack [18] . Such an agent can satisfy behaviorist formal safety guarantees and remain catastrophically dangerous in practice. For example, think of a robot that never takes a malign action with its actuators, but runs an internal computation which causes an unaligned successor agent to be copied into a different system.

This is not to say that we are to abandon abstraction. Indeed, it is implausible that the solution to the alignment problem must or should depend on, e.g., the details of the hardware or the operating system. Instead, we need to develop new abstractions which would be better suited for the problem at hand, abstractions that go beyond pure behaviorism.

Inner and Outer Alignment

So far I have described my preferred perspective on the alignment problem. A different frame, popular in the AI alignment community, is "inner and outer alignment". IMO the inner/outer alignment frame is less precise, but can still be a useful source of intuition. It is hence worthwhile to understand the connection between these views, and in particular to see how my perspective captures the "mesa-optimizer" threat model.

First, let me briefly recap what a mesa-optimizer is (following Hubinger et al. 2019). For the purpose of this argument, we are thinking of the agent as an episodic reinforcement learning algorithm. Then, a mesa-optimizer is a learned policy which is an agent in itself. Crucially, the mesa-optimizer might have a reward function different from that of the outer-loop reinforcement learner. There are two reasons why this might happen:

  • The inner (mesa-optimizer) reward might have been close to the outer reward on previous episodes, which "fooled" the outer-loop learning algorithm. This is consistent with the inner reward drastically departing from the outer reward in yet-unexplored regions of state-space.
  • The mesa-optimizer might be planning on a time horizon much longer than a single episode. In this case, it has the incentive to intentionally hide its misaligned preferences in order to be stabilized by the outer loop.

If the outer-loop learning algorithm is allowed to continue, it will either eventually remove the mesa-optimizer or force the mesa-optimizer to forever display behavior aligned with the outer reward. However, if the environment allows irreversible processes (as the real world does), then the mesa-optimizer can bide its time until an opportune moment to irreversibly push the system into a region of state-space favored by the inner reward (and typically unfavored by the outer reward). This is closely related to the "sharp left turn" of Soares 2022.

Under this model, "outer alignment" means that the outer reward function is close to that of the user, whereas "inner alignment" means that the inner reward function is (globally) close to the outer reward function. Each of them is a non-trivial problem.

A possible real-world example of mesa-optimization is the evolution of Homo sapiens. Arguably, we can model evolution as a reinforcement learning algorithm whose reward function is reproductive fitness. Evolution created humans who are agents (and in particular reinforcement learners), but the human reward function is different—if all we cared about were reproductive fitness, we would never have invented birth control (or at least, it would be much less popular). Given enough time, natural selection should be able to "fix" this, but it's probably never going to happen because human society and technology evolve much faster towards other ends, which is irreversible from evolution's vantage point.

Would addressing the problems in the previous sections address inner alignment as well? I argue that it would. If we had a guarantee that the agent's attributes are aligned, then, in particular, it wouldn't be controlled by a misaligned mesa-optimizer. These guarantees are supposed to take irreversible processes into account, so the "sharp left turn" is ruled out. These guarantees are supposed to include both direct effects and side-effects, ruling out both attack vectors for mesa-optimizers (in the terminology of the original LTA article, direct effects correspond to "Cartesian daemons" and side-effects to "non-Cartesian daemons").

More constructively, the outer vs. inner alignment dichotomy approximately corresponds to alignment of preferences vs. alignment of beliefs and decisions. Indeed, if we think of the outer loop as model-based reinforcement learning, then the learned policy comes from a learned model, in which case a misaligned inner agent corresponds to a misaligned belief. (For example, Christiano's argument that "the universal prior is malign" can be viewed as describing such a misaligned belief.) Alternatively, if we think of the outer loop as model-free reinforcement learning, then the misaligned inner agent corresponds to misaligned decision-making (although I think that the model-based view is more useful).

Conclusion

We have seen that solving the alignment problem requires a body of theory that can tackle the core challenges of the problem: alignment grounding, alignment convergence and side-channel resilience, in the context of holistic alignment and hypercomplexity. This taxonomy is not necessarily intended as a decomposition where each subproblem is possible to solve separately—while thinking of them as subproblems can be fruitful, ultimately they are interconnected. (For example, alignment grounding requires modeling the user as an agent, which requires understanding how agents deal with irreversible mistakes, which is a subproblem of alignment convergence.) It is intended as a set of lenses that must be applied to any proposed solution in order to validate its viability.

In the following posts we will discuss the emerging computational agent theory, and see how it is building the tools to address all of these difficulties.
